abstract: The function of hearing as an early warning system relies partly on detecting the distance and motion of an object based on sound. Approaching - or looming - objects activate the human alerting system, but it is debated whether sounds in the immediate vicinity of the body achieve the same irrespective of the direction of motion and of sound intensity. We addressed this question by examining distance perception of and phasic alertness states evoked by virtual sonic motion into and within peripersonal and extrapersonal space, at high and low intensities, in normal-hearing adults. Based on distance ratings, target detection promptness, and electroencephalography (EEG), we found that looming auditory objects increase phasic alertness and auditory sensory gain, and we also observed a general tendency to perceive sound offsets as closer to the body than onsets. However, we did not find evidence that auditory objects moving at a constant distance within peripersonal space affect alerting over and above the influence of intensity. We suggest that the auditory looming bias is not amplified further by preferential processing of auditory information near the body, and that the early warning function of hearing emphasizes the direction of motion over distance.
